metadata.file_name: Overcrowded Classrooms and their Association with South African Learners  Mathematics Achievement.pdf
metadata.title: Overcrowded Classrooms and their Association with South African Learners’ Mathematics Achievement
metadata.venue: African Journal of Research in Mathematics, Science and Technology Education

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses TIMSS 2019 South Africa data for Grade 9 mathematics, analyzed via the IEA IDB Analyzer. TIMSS employs a two-stage stratified cluster sampling design (schools sampled by size, then intact classes selected), which implies complex survey design features that are typically handled through TIMSS-provided sampling weights in IEA software. The manuscript does not report the specific weight variable name(s) or whether weights were explicitly applied in the analysis, so the exact weighting approach cannot be verified from the text. The quantitative analysis focuses on associations between class size (teacher-reported agreement with overcrowding and class size proxy items) and mathematics plausible values, while the qualitative phase uses purposive sampling in eight schools.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The dependent variable in the quantitative phase is TIMSS mathematics achievement measured using five plausible values, and the IEA IDB Analyzer is used to handle all five plausible values. However, the manuscript does not describe how missing data in predictors or questionnaire items were handled (e.g., whether cases with missing responses were excluded or whether any imputation was used). Given that TIMSS questionnaire items and teacher/classroom variables can have nonresponse, this omission is a reporting gap that limits reproducibility of the exact analytic sample construction.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Quantitative phase: secondary analysis of TIMSS 2019 for South Africa at Grade 9 mathematics. The realized TIMSS sample for South Africa comprises 519 schools, 543 mathematics and science teachers, and 20,829 learners; the manuscript does not report additional exclusions beyond the TIMSS sampling/realized sample. Qualitative phase: purposive sampling of principals and SP mathematics teachers in South African public schools—12 teachers in early interviews (March–September 2020) and later interviews with six principals and 12 teachers across six schools (with qualitative analysis spanning eight schools total, involving six principals and 24 teachers).

main_findings.performance_metrics: Correlation (BTBG10): r = -0.247, p < 0.001. t-test for BTB09A groups: reference 'Disagree a lot' mean PV = 413.08; 'Disagree a little' mean PV = 412.81 (difference -0.27, |t| = -0.02); 'Agree a little' mean PV = 396.33 (difference -16.75, |t| = -1.30); 'Agree a lot' mean PV = 378.50 (difference -34.58, |t| = -3.15).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TIMSS 2019 Grade 9 Mathematics (South Africa) the study leveraged class size (number of learners) and teachers’ agreement that there are too many learners in the class to analyze mathematics achievement (plausible values), finding that larger classes and stronger teacher perceptions of overcrowding were associated with lower mathematics achievement. This indicates that reducing classroom overcrowding and addressing teacher-reported overcrowding may improve mathematics outcomes, though the study is non-experimental so causal effects cannot be inferred.

data.outcome_summary: The study conducts a secondary analysis of TIMSS 2019 for South Africa at Grade 9 mathematics, using the TIMSS mathematics plausible values (five PVs) and analyzing associations between class size/overcrowding perceptions and mathematics achievement. Quantitatively, mathematics achievement shows a negative association with class size (BTBG10 correlation r = -0.247, p < 0.001). In group comparisons based on teacher agreement with the statement “There are too many learners in the class” (BTB09A), learners taught by teachers who “agree a lot” scored 34.58 points lower on average than the “disagree a lot” reference group (|t| = 3.15). Qualitatively, interviews in 2020–2021 (eight schools; six principals and 24 teachers) suggest mechanisms including limited individualized interaction, didactic neglect, and time management challenges. Limitations include non-experimental design (no causal identification) and incomplete reporting of missing-data handling and whether complex survey weights were explicitly applied.
